chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Studio categories: Black jazz players versus lead players
summary: Studios categorized players; Ernie Royal was the exception as a Black lead player.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, look at Clark Terry. He was a famous jazz player. Twenty years a studio musician. Stan Getz did it for a number of years and he only loused himself

The only thing was that studio -- the studio worked just like everybody else, they had categories. And I know that if you were a black musician you were a jazz player and you didn't get too much calls to be a lead player. E ie Royal was an exception because he was a great high note player and they always had to have him because he was the best around on that. But it worked both ways. If they were going to have a white guy who played perfectly good jazz and maybe not very good lead, they would call in a black guy who was a hell of a good lead player and maybe didn't play very good jazz -- but he played jazz and you played lead.

But most studio players, you know, had some kind of training and they could do all kinds of work, you know. They took lessons and tried to improve themselves. And I think the put-down term came from the musicians who didn't take lessons and improve themselves and were a little jealous.

Because I used to get criticism from even guys in the studio saying, you know, you've been taking lessons, that's really sort of taking unfair advantage. Honest to God, another trumpet player in New York said that to me. So in the beginning, they sort of did that.
